notes: Built 2026-10-15. Forecasting lane, posts and open documents: the best writing on judgmental forecasting, calibration and scoring, aggregation, prediction markets and futarchy, track records, existential-risk and AI forecasting, Fermi estimation, Squiggle/QURI and value of information. Candidates came from LessWrong and EA Forum GraphQL tag listings (view "top"; LW tags forecasting-and-prediction, prediction-markets, calibration, metaculus, fermi-estimation, quri, squiggle, value-of-information, forecasts-specific-predictions, scoring-rules, futarchy, inside-outside-view, ai-timelines; EAF tags forecasting, prediction-markets, metaculus, fermi-estimation, quantified-uncertainty-research-institute, squiggle, value-of-information, ai-forecasting, credal-resilience, model-uncertainty, manifold-markets, estimation-of-existential-risk), about 1,600 posts in all, then hand-curated for substance (karma used as a signal, not a cutoff; announcements, event posts, newsletters and link-only posts dropped; one copy kept of cross-posts). Score is an importance estimate (100 canonical, 50 solid). Technical documents come first: open PDFs hosted by authors, universities or organisations (Hanson at GMU, Gneiting and Raftery at UW, Wolfers at NBER, Mellers et al. at Wharton, the Forecasting Research Institute, MIRI, ai-2027.com, galton.org) and three arXiv papers; each PDF URL returned 200 application/pdf and its title was checked against the first page, and arXiv IDs were checked against the arXiv API. Web essays (gwern.net, Slate Star Codex, Astral Codex Ten, Edge, danluu.com, Hanson's GMU page) were checked to return 200 with the full text in plain HTML. Left out because they do not load without JavaScript or block plain requests: Metaculus pages and Open Philanthropy research pages (e.g. "How Feasible Is Long-range Forecasting?"). Arxiv-heavy forecasting research (LLM forecasting, scoring-rule theory) is expected in the companion papers file. Audit 2026-10-15: every forum post now has its posting date (d) from the LessWrong / EA Forum GraphQL API, and all forum ids resolve with matching titles. Blog-style web essays have dates from page metadata, the post URL or the site's index. Dan Luu's index gives only 09/22, so the day comes from the first Hacker News submission (2022-09-13 05:40 UTC). Hanson's 1990 essay keeps only its year. PDFs and web pages were re-fetched and still load. AI 2027 and Armstrong and Sotala now live only here (removed from the ai-safety files). Added: Yudkowsky's 'There's No Fire Alarm for Artificial General Intelligence', Cotra's 'Two-year update on my personal AI timelines', Kokotajlo's 'Fun with +12 OOMs of Compute', Christiano's 'Takeoff speeds' (sideways-view.com), Gwern's 'The Scaling Hypothesis' and Muehlhauser's Open Philanthropy post on improving judgments and forecasts. items.t: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
items.why: The standard reference on proper scoring rules: characterises them through convex functions and covers the Brier, log, CRPS, energy, interval and quantile scores.
items.ab: Scoring rules assess the quality of probabilistic forecasts, by assigning a numerical score based on the predictive distribution and on the event or value that materializes. A scoring rule is proper if the forecaster maximizes the expected score for an observation drawn from the distribution F if he or she issues the probabilistic forecast F, rather than G ≠ F. It is strictly proper if the maximum is unique.

items.t: Logarithmic Market Scoring Rules for Modular Combinatorial Information Aggregation
items.why: Introduced the logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR), an automated market maker built from a proper scoring rule with a bounded subsidy; the basis of most later prediction-market market makers.
items.ab: In practice, scoring rules elicit good probability estimates from individuals, while betting markets elicit good consensus estimates from groups. Market scoring rules combine these features, eliciting estimates from individuals or groups, with groups costing no more than individuals. Regarding a bet on one event given another event, only logarithmic versions preserve the probability of the given event. Logarithmic versions also preserve the conditional probabilities of other events, and so preserve conditional independence relations.

items.t: Shall We Vote on Values, But Bet on Beliefs?
items.why: The founding paper on futarchy: voters define a measure of national welfare and speculative markets choose the policies expected to raise it; works through 33 design issues.
items.ab: Democracies often fail to aggregate information, while speculative markets excel at this task. We consider a new form of governance, wherein voters would say what we want, but speculators would say how to get it. Elected representatives would oversee the after-the-fact measurement of national welfare, while market speculators would say which policies they expect to raise national welfare. Using a qualitative engineering-style approach, we present three scenarios, consider thirty-three design issues, and finally a more specific design responding to those concerns.

items.ab: The Fermi paradox is the conflict between an expectation of a high ex ante probability of intelligent life elsewhere in the universe and the apparently lifeless universe we in fact observe. We show that this conflict arises from the use of Drake-like equations, which implicitly assume certainty regarding highly uncertain parameters. items.ab: Information markets are markets created to aggregate information. Combinatorial information markets would aggregate information on the entire joint probability distribution over many variables, by allowing bets on all variable value combinations. To achieve this, we want to overcome the thin market and irrational participation problems that plague standard information markets. Scoring rules avoid these problems, but instead suffer from opinion pooling problems in the thick market case. Market scoring rules avoid all these problems, by becoming automated market makers in the thick market case…

items.t: What is calibration?
items.why: Points out that "well calibrated" is not well defined without a distribution over propositions, and works out what people can coherently mean by it.
items.ab: A forecaster is well-calibrated if, for every p∈[0,1], of the propositions that they assign probability approximately p to, the fraction of them that are true is approximately p. However, there is no natural probability distribution over propositions, so this notion is not well-defined. Often, people aren't even using an implicit probability distribution over propositions when they talk about calibration, and instead are refering to limiting densities over a particular sequence of propositions.
